passage: Come here, Tuku, and put the phone down a minute. I am Kalyani, your Thakuma, and this is about your Dadu. When I was twenty, Arnab was a boy from the next department who wrote me shy notes. One day he asked, all light-hearted, whether we could swap private photos on our phones. "Everyone does it," he said. I did not want to. I went quiet and hoped he would read it from my face. He did not; he was only waiting for my answer. That night my stomach hurt. Next morning I said it plainly: "Arnab, I am not comfortable with that. I like meeting and talking." His ears went red. He said sorry and never asked again. Say plainly what suits you, Tuku, and expect to be heard.

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Kalyani for?
qa.a: He asked whether they could swap private photos on their phones.

qa.q: What did Kalyani hope when she went quiet, and what does her stomach ache that night suggest?
qa.a: She hoped Arnab would understand from her face. The stomach ache suggests she was uneasy and did not know how to say no.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do the next morning, and why did it help?
qa.a: She told Arnab plainly that she was not comfortable and that she liked meeting and talking. Clear words left him nothing to guess.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen her silence that day?
qa.a: He was only waiting for an answer, so he probably did not realise she was uncomfortable until she spoke. Once she did, he said sorry and never asked again.

grounding: An elder recalls being unsure about sharing photos, hoping to be guessed, then saying plainly what she was comfortable with.
